answer_raw:
Morning-type people tend to report higher levels of happiness and life satisfaction than night owls [1][2][7].

The correlation between morningness and happiness is often linked to better sleep quality, as morning types are often naturally aligned with their own circadian rhythms [1]. While they report feeling more **cheerful, lively, and alert**, they do not necessarily report lower levels of distress or nervousness than night owls [2]. It is also important to note that these findings do not support a blanket claim that every single early riser is happier than every night owl [2].

A shift in tendencies can occur as people age, as the "night owl" tendencies seen in teenagers often **fade with age** [7]. This transition toward a more morning-focused schedule may contribute to why older adults often report higher levels of happiness than younger generations [7]. There is no specific evidence in the provided research regarding whether a person can manually "switch" their chronotype through lifestyle changes, though the data suggests natural shifts happen over time.
